summary: An update from BBN on the attempt to release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15, 1972, which failed. The main causes were that the network had grown too large to coordinate operator action at every site, and that IMPs running the old and new systems disturbed each other. BBN planned new attempts. It was replaced by RFC 359.

plainLanguage.summary: BBN reports that its May 15 attempt to release IMPSYS 2600 failed because coordination across the network was difficult and old and new IMP systems interfered with each other. It asked sites to prepare for repeated attempts, and RFC 359 later replaced this notice.

questions: why did the impsys 2600 release fail
when were the next impsys release attempts planned
subtitle: A notice explaining why the May 1972 IMP software release failed

tldr.problem: The attempted release of IMPSYS 2600 on May 15 did not succeed.
tldr.mechanism: BBN attributed the failure to difficulty coordinating operators across the larger network and to interference between adjacent IMPs running different systems.
tldr.outcome: The notice scheduled another attempt for May 31 and then each Tuesday until success; RFC 359 later replaced it.

sections.title: Why the Release Failed
sections.content:
BBN's attempt to release IMPSYS 2600 on May 15 was unsuccessful. The RFC says the causes were operational rather than programming bugs.

The network had grown too large for BBN to coordinate operator intervention at every site. In addition, IMPs running the new system were affected by adjacent IMPs running the old system, and the reverse also occurred. BBN called this the poisoning effect.
sections.plainLanguage: The upgrade failed for two operational reasons: BBN could not coordinate every site easily, and neighboring machines running different versions interfered with one another.

sections.title: Preparation for Another Attempt
sections.content:
BBN asked sites with Model 516 IMPs to keep four named switches in specified positions. It also asked sites not to use the IMP Trace routine during release days. Terminal IMPs could be turned off for significant parts of those days.

The next attempt was scheduled for Wednesday, May 31, followed by attempts every Tuesday until the release succeeded. BBN expected to begin early in the day, approximately 7 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time, and suggested that sites avoid scheduling production work over the network during an attempt.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN gave sites switch settings and asked them to avoid certain activities during the upgrade. It planned to retry on May 31 and each Tuesday after that until the release worked.

sections.title: Purpose of the Notice
sections.content:
This RFC asks network sites to cooperate with the planned release and explains why the previous attempt took longer than expected. BBN said operator coverage was not required for the planned process, but hoped it would be available if unexpected problems arose.

The unit metadata records RFC 359 as the successor to this notification.
sections.plainLanguage: The notice tells operators what BBN learned and what it asked them to do next. RFC 359 later replaced it.

references.text: RFC 331, describing the earlier attempt to release IMPSYS 2600.
